raw_case_text:
A 17 year old male patient with no previous comorbidities presented with a 13 day history of high grade fever and productive cough. The patient also had nausea and vomiting for 7 days, followed by bilateral flank and epigastric pain for 5 days. The patient was initially treated for dengue fever (Dengue NS1 test positive) at rural health care facilities in Kashmir. The patient developed sinus bradycardia, heart rate of 37 beats per minute, with borderline blood pressures of 100/70 mmHg that was managed with Atropine and transferred to the tertiary care hospital in Islamabad. On admission, patient was afebrile with normal liver function tests, thyroid profile, Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies (ANCA) profile and Extractable Nuclear Antigen Antibodies (ENA) profile. Further workup revealed weakly positive (Antinuclear Antibody) ANA and elevated serum creatinine of 1.5 mg/dL (0.5-1.0 mg/dL) which was presumed to be pre-renal acute kidney injury. Baseline Hemoglobin was 14.7 g/dL, White blood cell count 4350/uL, and Platelets of 140 thousand/uL. On day 2 of admission he was started on intravenous fluids and empirical antibiotics. On the 3rd day of admission, patient developed apprehension. 12 lead ECG was done along with cardiac enzymes. Cardiac enzymes were found to be elevated with Troponin I of 2610 pg/mL and CKMB 9 %, however ECG did not reveal any specific ischemic changes. Echocardiography performed on day 2 of admission was consistent with reduced LV systolic function of 35 % with mild tricuspid and pulmonary regurgitation, along with mid-ventricular ballooning and hyperdynamic apices depicting reverse takotsubo syndrome [Fig. 1]. Patient was shifted to critical care unit thereon for cardiac monitoring. He was started on guideline directed medical therapy for cardiomyopathy.
During his stay in critical care unit the patient developed sinus bradycardia (heart rate ranging between 40 and 60 beats per minute, which did not require Atropine) with hypotension. Hypotension was largely attributed to hypovolemia, which resolved with careful intravenous fluid resuscitation. IV fluids were discontinued after adequate oral intake was established. Bradycardia improved sequentially.
Repeat echocardiography was performed after 72 h which revealed same ejection fraction as before. Patients blood and urine culture were sent to the lab and revealed no microbial growth. At the time of discharge patient was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. His cardiac enzymes had improved with Troponin I down to 862 pg/mL and CKMB 3.4 %. Labs revealed improved serum creatinine of 1.25 mg/dL. His bradycardia had fully resolved and he was discharged with a plan for follow up echocardiography after 5 days. Discharge medications included Valsartan tablet 40 mg once daily (OD), Aspirin 75 mg tablet OD and a multivitamin tablet 22.5 mg OD all to be taken orally for a month.
Furthermore, he was found to be Vitamin D deficient (Vit D levels 6 ng/mL - Normal range 20-50 ng/mL), therefore a Vitamin-D3 cholecalciferol tablet once daily was added to his prescription. For persistent dyspepsia Tablet Omeprazole 40 mg tablet OD was also prescribed to be taken orally for 14 days. Tablet Valsartan 40 mg and tablet Aspirin 75 mg were continued on once daily dosage. On follow up 5 days after discharge repeat echocardiography showed complete reversion to normal left ventricle function and improvement of ejection fraction to 60 %.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old male presented with a 13-day history of high-grade fever and productive cough, followed by nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 13-day history of high-grade fever and productive cough, accompanied by nausea and vomiting for 7 days, and bilateral flank and epigastric pain for 5 days. He was managed initially at a regional clinic where he developed severe sinus bradycardia (heart rate 37 bpm) and hypotension (100/70 mmHg) treated with atropine before transfer. On hospital day 3, he developed sudden apprehension.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported fever, productive cough, nausea, vomiting, epigastric and flank pain, and persistent dyspepsia. Denied chest pain or syncope.

objective.physical_examination: Upon tertiary admission, the patient was afebrile with borderline blood pressure of 100/70 mmHg and sinus bradycardia (heart rate ranging between 37 and 60 bpm). Cardiovascular and chest examinations were otherwise without overt signs of congestion.
objective.routine_investigations:
Complete blood count: Hemoglobin 14.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 4,350/muL, platelet count 140,000/muL.
Renal function & biochemistry: Serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL (reference: 0.5-1.0 mg/dL, normalized to 1.25 mg/dL), normal liver function tests, normal thyroid function profile, serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D 6 ng/mL (reference: 20-50 ng/mL).
Cardiac biomarkers: Day 3 Troponin I 2,610 pg/mL and CK-MB 9% (decreased to Troponin I 862 pg/mL and CK-MB 3.4% at discharge).
Autoimmune serology: Weakly positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA); negative ANCA and ENA panels.
Microbiology: Blood and urine cultures yielded no microbial growth.
Electrocardiogram: Sinus bradycardia without acute ST-T wave ischemic changes.
Transthoracic echocardiogram: Admission revealed reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 35%, mild tricuspid and pulmonary regurgitation, and mid-ventricular ballooning with hyperdynamic apices consistent with reverse Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Follow-up echocardiogram at 5 days post-discharge showed complete normalization of left ventricular function with LVEF 60%.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue-induced reverse Takotsubo cardiomyopathy with sinus bradycardia and pre-renal acute kidney injury, confirmed by positive dengue NS1 antigen test. Ruled out systemic autoimmune vasculitis/connective tissue disease (negative ANCA/ENA), thyroid dysfunction, and bacterial sepsis (negative blood/urine cultures).
Treatment and outcome: Managed in CCU with careful intravenous crystalloid resuscitation, empiric antibiotics, oral valsartan (40 mg daily), aspirin (75 mg daily), oral omeprazole (40 mg daily), and vitamin D3 supplementation. Bradycardia and renal dysfunction resolved completely, and cardiac function fully normalized to LVEF 60% on follow-up echocardiogram.
